newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended with slight gains on scale-down roaster buying. November added $5 to close at $1,541, while January was up $5 at $1,461 per tonne. The nearby November/January spread stood at $85, almost the same as Thursday's close.

In New York arabica futures ended mixed with nearby December down 1.50 cents/lb at 125.86 cents/lb. March lost 50 points to close at 111.85 cents/lb. However, the lack of deliverable supplies and a general lack of available physical coffee for the near term remained supportive and should serve to limit the downside. Traders said the question is how long the tightness will persist. Most analysts seem to be convinced that supply will remain tight into early December.

ACPC - The technical group of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) held a meeting in Costa Rica on November 9. Even though no decision has been made at the meeting because the technical group can only propose changes to the full ACPC Council, the members, which group the globe's biggest producer nations and the 14-member council accounts for more than 80 per cent of world output, made it clear that they want to keep the squeeze on coffee supplies.

ACPC nations have in place a coffee export programme to limit green coffee exports to 53.3 million 60-kg bags in 1996/97 (July/June) compared to 45.8 million bags the previous year. Jorge Cardenas, head of Colombia's National Coffee Growers Federation, said earlier changes to the export limits would aim at curbing the effects of a surge in supply during the first three to five months of 1997 after recent tightness.

However, ACPC secretary-general Robeiro Oliveira ruled out any immediate modification in the export targets. He suggested any modifications would only be made at the ACPC's February meeting in Colombia or Indonesia. But he agreed with Cardenas in saying that the first half of the new year was crucial to the ACPC's bid to regulate world supply.

The ACPC is confident that supplies will remain tight. Production in 1996/97 is estimated at 99 million bags while consumption in 1996/97 (October/September) is put at 100 million bags of which 75 million bags in consuming countries and 25 million bags in producing countries. Offtake in 1995/96 was put at 96.9 million bags. Against this background, it is believed, there is only one way for prices and that is up.

SINGAPORE - Singapore imported 702,000 bags of coffee in January/June 1996, 25 per cent less than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped to 1.9 million bags down from 2.9 million bags in 1994.

The main supplier in January/June 1996 was Vietnam with 116,200 bags against 391,500 bags the same period in 1995. However, not only imports but also exports are down. The total in January/June 1996 reached 715,800 bags, 27 per cent less than was exported the same period in 1995.
Total exports in calendar year 1995 dropped sharply to 1.9 million bags from 2.8 million bags the previous year.

COLOMBIA - Personal consumption of coffee in Colombia has dropped 21.15 per cent in the last ten years, according to the Colombian National Coffee Growers Federation. However, consumption remained fairly high at 9.6 cups per household but that is down from 12.7 in 1987.
